scenes.title: Architecture of the second brain
scenes.subtitle: Your gut contains a complete nervous system — 500 million neurons, more than the spinal cord.

scenes.title: Enteric network
scenes.subtitle: It wraps the entire digestive tract in a dense mesh of sensory neurons, interneurons, and motor neurons.

scenes.title: Independent origin
scenes.subtitle: These neurons did not grow from your brain. They migrated from the neural crest during early embryonic development.

scenes.title: Long migration
scenes.subtitle: Neural crest cells travel from the closing neural tube down into the developing gut, building a second brain from a different source.

scenes.title: Independence
scenes.subtitle: The enteric nervous system can function without any input from the brain or spinal cord.

scenes.title: Peristaltic reflex
scenes.subtitle: An isolated segment of gut can coordinate peristalsis entirely on its own. Cut it free and it still moves food.

scenes.title: Local decision
scenes.subtitle: Sensory neurons detect stretch. Interneurons process the signal. Motor neurons contract the muscle downstream. All in the gut.

scenes.title: Serotonin factory
scenes.subtitle: The gut produces 95 percent of the body's serotonin — the molecule most associated with mood, well-being, and emotion.

scenes.title: Mood molecule
scenes.subtitle: Most of the serotonin in your blood was made by enteric neurons, not by your brain.

scenes.title: Gut-brain chemistry
scenes.subtitle: The gut synthesizes serotonin from dietary tryptophan and releases it into the bloodstream and the brain.

scenes.title: The vagus highway
scenes.subtitle: The vagus nerve connects the gut and the brain, carrying signals in both directions.

scenes.title: Eighty percent ascending
scenes.subtitle: Eighty to ninety percent of vagal fibers carry information from the body upward to the brainstem.

scenes.title: Bottom-up perception
scenes.subtitle: Your brain does not merely command the body. It listens to the body, and most of what it hears comes from the gut.

scenes.title: Microbiome dialogue
scenes.subtitle: The gut microbiome produces neurotransmitters that enteric neurons detect and relay.

scenes.title: Bacterial signaling
scenes.subtitle: Gut bacteria synthesize dopamine, serotonin, GABA, and other molecules that influence mood and behavior.

scenes.title: Ecosystem inside
scenes.subtitle: Your gut hosts an ecosystem of trillions of microorganisms. They talk to your second brain, and your second brain talks to your first.

scenes.title: Gut feelings are real
scenes.subtitle: Interoception — the perception of internal body states — carries enteric signals into conscious awareness.

scenes.title: Insula integration
scenes.subtitle: The insular cortex maps the body's internal state. It is where the gut feeling becomes a felt sensation.

scenes.title: Intuition has anatomy
scenes.subtitle: What we call intuition may be the enteric nervous system contributing its computation to decisions before the brain has finished processing.

scenes.title: Enteric glia
scenes.subtitle: More than half of the cells in the enteric nervous system are glia — support cells that maintain neuronal health.

scenes.title: Gut barrier
scenes.subtitle: Enteric glia help maintain the gut barrier and regulate inflammation. They are the immune system's interface with the enteric brain.

scenes.title: Trophic support
scenes.subtitle: Glial cells release neurotrophic factors that keep enteric neurons alive and functional throughout life.

scenes.title: Stress reshapes the gut
scenes.subtitle: Chronic stress alters enteric neural activity, barrier function, and gut motility.

scenes.title: Vagal withdrawal
scenes.subtitle: Stress suppresses vagal tone, disconnecting the two brains and leaving the gut to operate without higher modulation.

scenes.title: Healing the connection
scenes.subtitle: Restoring vagal tone through breath, movement, or social connection improves enteric function and emotional regulation.

scenes.title: Lifelong neurogenesis
scenes.subtitle: Unlike most of the central nervous system, the enteric nervous system continues to generate new neurons throughout life.

scenes.title: Continuous renewal
scenes.subtitle: The enteric brain is not a fixed structure. It rewires, replaces, and adapts in response to diet, experience, and injury.

scenes.title: Two brains, one body
scenes.subtitle: The cephalic brain and the enteric brain are separate organs with different embryological origins, different transmitters, different functio

scenes.title: Parallel processing
scenes.subtitle: They process information in parallel, communicate bidirectionally, and influence each other's development.

scenes.title: Second mind
scenes.subtitle: The enteric nervous system has its own sensory processing, its own reflexes, its own memory, its own capacity to learn.

scenes.title: Intelligence is distributed
scenes.subtitle: Intelligence is not a single organ. It is distributed throughout the body, and the body has ways of knowing the brain does not.

scenes.title: Embodied cognition
scenes.subtitle: Cognition is not computation on abstract symbols. It is the activity of a body that senses, moves, digests, and feels.

scenes.title: Listen
scenes.subtitle: The voice inside your chest is not a metaphor. It is a neural network with half a billion neurons speaking in the language of serotonin and

scenes.title: Resilience
scenes.subtitle: The enteric nervous system repairs itself, adapts to injury, and maintains function across decades of use.

scenes.title: Neuroplasticity
scenes.subtitle: Enteric neuroplasticity is the reason dietary changes, probiotics, and behavioral interventions can reshape gut function.

scenes.title: Supported claims
scenes.subtitle: That the gut has an independent nervous system. That it produces most of the body's serotonin. That it communicates with the brain.

scenes.title: Emerging frontier
scenes.subtitle: That gut feelings are interoceptive signals reaching awareness. That the microbiome modulates mood. These are active research frontiers.

scenes.title: Not metaphor
scenes.subtitle: What traditions called the second brain or the voice in the chest is now visible as a biological organ with specific anatomy and physiology.

scenes.title: Final frame
scenes.subtitle: Listen to the voice inside your chest. It has been trying to tell you something.
